title: Direction-dependent magnetoelectric conductivity from dipolar topological semimetals
abstract: We compute the linear magnetoelectric conductivity of a two-band vortex nodal-ring (VNR) semimetal and a three-band Hopf semimetal (HSM) within the semiclassical Boltzmann formalism in the relaxation-time approximation. We consider three inequivalent planar-Hall configurations, in which the electric ($\boldsymbol E$) and magnetic ($\boldsymbol B$) fields are oriented differently with respect to the nodal-ring plane and the BC-dipole axis. Unlike Weyl and multifold semimetals, where Berry-curvature (BC) flux originates from monopole-like sources, both systems host dipole-like BC sources and vanishing Chern numbers. Working consistently to cubic order in the magnetic field, we evaluate the Drude, BC, orbital-magnetic-moment (OMM), anomalous-Hall, and Lorentz-force contributions to the conductivity. In both systems, the dipolar BC and OMM generate odd powers of $|\boldsymbol B|$ in in-plane response channels that are symmetry-forbidden in systems with monopole-like BC sources. For the HSM, the internode-scattering contribution to the conductivity vanishes identically. By comparing the VNR with a $\mathcal{PT}$-broken gapped nodal ring and the HSM with a pseudospin-1 triple-point semimetal, we demonstrate that the dipolar nature of the BC gives rise to distinctive features in magnetoelectric response that are absent in semimetals with monopole-like BC flux.
summary: This theoretical work calculates the magnetoelectric conductivity in nodal semimetals, focusing on the difference between dipole-like and monopole-like Berry curvature sources. It demonstrates that systems with dipolar topology, like VNR and HSM, exhibit unique, symmetry-forbidden magnetoelectric responses compared to standard Weyl semimetals. This highlights the importance of the underlying topological structure in determining measurable transport properties.
main_problem: The paper computes the linear magnetoelectric conductivity in planar-Hall geometries for topological semimetals, specifically contrasting systems with dipolar versus monopole-like Berry curvature sources.
main_result: The dipolar nature of the Berry curvature and Orbital Magnetic Moment (OMM) generates unique, symmetry-forbidden odd powers of the magnetic field in the in-plane conductivity channels, which is absent in systems with monopole-like sources.
method: The calculations employ the semiclassical Boltzmann formalism within the relaxation-time approximation, evaluating contributions from Drude, BC, OMM, anomalous-Hall, and Lorentz-force terms.
model_or_system: The study analyzes two primary models: the two-band Vortex Nodal-Ring (VNR) semimetal and the three-band Hopf Semimetal (HSM). Comparisons are drawn with Weyl semimetals (monopole sources) and other nodal systems.
key_observables: Linear magnetoelectric conductivity ($\sigma_{lf}$), Berry curvature flux (dipolar vs. monopole), and the presence of odd powers of $|B|$ in in-plane response channels.
important_parameters: Cubic order in the magnetic field ($B^3$), and the specific planar-Hall field configurations.
main_assumptions: Calculations are performed using the semiclassical Boltzmann formalism and assume static, uniform electric and magnetic fields.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the smoke-ring pattern of the vector field $\mathbf{d}(\mathbf{k})$ near a VNR section. Figure 2 compares the BC field near a TSM (monopole-like) versus an HSM (dipolar, zero net flux).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the conductivity in different planar-Hall setups, comparing the VNR and HSM models. It details the vanishing of certain contributions (e.g., internode scattering in HSM) and contrasts the resulting magnetoelectric response with known monopole-like systems.
why_interesting: The focus on geometric properties like Berry curvature dipoles and their direct, measurable impact on transport coefficients (magnetoelectric response) provides a concrete link between advanced topological invariants and observable condensed matter phenomena.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Pictorial depiction of some unique features of VNRs: (a) Dispersion E against the kxky-plane showing two bands crossing along a circle (highlighted in green), setting kz = 0. (b) Nature of the vector fields d(k) [or, equivalently, d0(k) in the vicinity of the VNR] and Ωs=2(k) in the vicinity of a section of the toroidal Fermi surface (gray). The former displays a smoke-ring pattern.

FIG. 2. Pictorial depiction of some unique features of HSMs and TSMs: (a) Dispersion E against the kxky-plane showing two bands crossing at the nodal point (highlighted in green), setting kz = 0, and the flat-band (highlighted in yellow). (b) Monopole-like BC field near the node of a TSM with C = ±2, exhibiting a net outward flux, and the dipolar BC field near the node of an HSM (C = 0), characterised by opposite field lines in the two hemispheres and vanishing total flux through the sphere.

FIG. 3. The three inequivalent planar-Hall configurations analysed in this work, shown relative to the kz = 0 plane and the Cartesian coordinates with unit vectors (ˆx, ˆy, ˆz). Red and blue arrows denote the applied electric (E) and magnetic (B) fields, respectively. Set-up I: E = Ex ˆx, B = Bx ˆx+By ˆy. Set-up II: E = Ex ˆx, B = Bx ˆx+Bz ˆz. Set-up III: E = Ez ˆz, B = Bx ˆx+Bz ˆz. In each set-up, θ denotes the angle between B and the x-axis, so that Bx = |B| cos θ together with By = |B| sin θ in set-up I, or Bz = |B| sin θ in set-ups II and III.

FIG. 4. Set-up I for VNR: Behaviour of conductivity curves (in eV) as functions of e B v2 0/µ2 and θ. Here we have omitted showing the σah yx curve as its order of magnitude is highly incompatible with the remaining curves.

FIG. 5. Set-up II for VNR: Behaviour of the conductivity curves (in eV) as functions of e B v2 0/µ2 and θ. For σyx, we have omitted showing the θ-dependence, and both panels show the field-strength dependence of the AH and LFO parts instead.
